title: Admin access requires mutual TLS and an IAM-bound identity
statement: Every fabric admin API or CLI call must be authenticated with mutual TLS and authorised against an IAM-bound workload or operator identity, and must be refused otherwise.
rationale: Admin operations can move leadership, change retention and isolate streams; an unauthenticated admin surface is a way to rewrite what the platform remembers.

sources.section: §7 Rust Fabric component rows — fabric-admin ('mTLS and IAM-bound access')

verification.check: Call each admin operation without a client certificate, with a valid certificate but an identity lacking the IAM binding, and with a bound identity, and assert only the last succeeds and every attempt is audited.

notes: Split from the fabric-admin row. Fabric admin access grants no authority over autonomy or risk limits (risk and execution domain rule). NEW_DEPENDENCY follows FABRIC-009's TLS class; MANAGED_SERVICE is for IAM.

title: The fabric exports native OpenTelemetry metrics, traces and health
statement: fabric-observe must export broker, metadata and mirror metrics, traces and health natively in OpenTelemetry form, each metric recorded at the seam where its fact becomes known.
rationale: Lag, under-replication and quorum latency are the fabric's early warnings; without them the first sign of trouble is a consumer that fell behind.

sources.section: §7 Rust Fabric component rows — fabric-observe ('Native OTel metrics')
§26 Recommended Build Order — Phase 2 Rust Fabric MVP ('OTel')

verification.check: Run a test cluster with an in-memory telemetry receiver and assert every documented fabric metric has at least one data point after a produce/consume/failover cycle, recorded by a non-test caller.

notes: Split from the fabric-observe row, whose liveness clause is FABRIC-073; G p22 is cited on verification for the MVP exit. ADR 0026 rejected an OpenTelemetry crate and ADR 0028/0032 settled the export path; the flag marks that native OTel emission needs that in-tree path or a record. House observability rule: a metric an alert names must have a recording site, which is what the check asserts.

title: Fabric health never depends on the fabric's own topics
statement: Fabric liveness and health must be observable through direct OpenTelemetry export and health endpoints and must not rely on the fabric's own event topics; the P4 Telemetry class is never the primary health path.
rationale: A monitor carried by the thing it monitors goes silent exactly when it is needed.

sources.section: §7 Rust Fabric component rows — fabric-observe ('does not rely on its own event topics for liveness')
§7.2 Fabric topic classes — P4 Telemetry row ('direct OTel remains primary health path')

verification.check: Stop every broker in a test cluster and assert the fabric's health endpoints and telemetry exporter still report the outage.

notes: Merges the fabric-observe liveness clause with the P4 row's health-path clause. NEW_DEPENDENCY is removed: the invariant concerns the path, and export is FABRIC-072's concern.

title: Bulk mirror transport is chosen by benchmark, TCP included
statement: For specific long-lived bulk mirror flows, TCP must be benchmarked against QUIC and the transport chosen by measurement rather than by assuming one protocol wins everywhere; mutual TLS is required either way.
rationale: Long-lived bulk flows are where QUIC's advantages matter least and a kernel TCP path may win; measuring avoids paying for an assumption.

sources.section: §7.1 Wire, ordering and delivery semantics — Transport ('Benchmark TCP for specific long-lived bulk mirror flows')

verification.check: fabric-bench compares mutually authenticated QUIC and TCP on a representative cross-region bulk mirror flow, and the recorded choice matches the measured throughput and tail latency.

notes: Stated twice in the raw extraction. Differs from v11.6, which names QUIC/mTLS for cross-region mirror traffic without qualification (M p36, FABRIC-009). v2.1 is the more specific and governs how the platform runs on Google Cloud (blueprint precedence), so a measured TCP choice for bulk mirror flows is permitted. NEW_DEPENDENCY is removed as inapplicable to the benchmark.

title: Partitions are chosen by an explicit ordering key
statement: Every produce must name an explicit ordering key, and all records with the same key on a topic must land in the same partition.
rationale: Ordering is only per partition (FABRIC-039); an explicit key is how a producer says which records must stay ordered, rather than hoping a default partitioner agrees.

sources.section: §7.1 Wire, ordering and delivery semantics — Partitioning ('explicit ordering key')

verification.check: Property test: for any set of keys and any sequence of produces, all records sharing a key sit in one partition and appear in produce order.

notes: Split from §7.1 Partitioning, whose leader-assignment clause is FABRIC-076 and replication clause FABRIC-010.

title: Partition leaders are placed by rendezvous or consistent assignment
statement: Partition leadership must be assigned to brokers by rendezvous or consistent-hash assignment, so adding or removing a broker moves only the partitions that must move.
rationale: A naive modulo assignment reshuffles every partition when a broker is added, turning a scale-out into a cluster-wide failover.

sources.section: §7.1 Wire, ordering and delivery semantics — Partitioning ('rendezvous/consistent assignment to partition leaders')

verification.check: Property test: adding one broker to an n-broker cluster moves roughly 1/(n+1) of leaderships, and no leadership moves between two brokers present both before and after.

notes: Stated twice in the raw extraction. P1: it matters when brokers are added (FABRIC-092), which the single-region MVP does not require.

title: A quorum ack means a majority persisted it, and no quorum-acked record is lost to a broker or zone failure
statement: A quorum acknowledgement must be issued only after a majority of the partition's RF3 replicas has persisted the record, so that a single broker or a whole zone can fail without losing any quorum-acknowledged P0, P1 or P2 record.
rationale: An acknowledgement is a promise producers act on: a fill acknowledged and then lost is a position the ledger never sees.

sources.section: §7.1 Wire, ordering and delivery semantics — Durability ('A quorum acknowledgment means the record survived on a majority of replicas')
§17 Availability, Resilience and Disaster Recovery — Fabric broker row ('Quorum-acked records preserved')
§27 Architecture Acceptance Criteria — 'A Fabric broker/zone can fail without losing quorum-acknowledged P0/P1/P2 records'

verification.check: On a three-zone cluster under random broker kills, zone partitions and restarts, record every acknowledged write and assert after healing that each is present in its partition, in order, on the current leader.

notes: Merges §7.1's quorum definition, the broker-failure row's recovery clause and the §27 acceptance criterion; they state one guarantee from its definition and its consequence. The §27 item's 'or stopping Reflex execution' is FABRIC-003. MULTI_REGION, NEW_DEPENDENCY and KUBERNETES, carried by those items, are removed as inapplicable.

title: Append batches are atomic within one partition
statement: A batch appended to one partition must become visible atomically: consumers see all of its records or none, never a prefix.
rationale: A producer batches records that belong together; a torn batch replays as half an event.

sources.section: §7.1 Wire, ordering and delivery semantics — Atomicity ('atomic append batches within one partition')

verification.check: Property test: crash the leader at arbitrary points during batch appends and assert no consumer ever observes a strict prefix of a batch.

notes: Split from the §7.1 Atomicity bullet, whose cross-partition clause is FABRIC-079.

title: Cross-partition business transactions are sagas, not broker transactions
statement: A business transaction spanning partitions must be represented as an explicit saga of commands and compensations recorded as ordinary records; the fabric must not offer, and nothing may rely on, hidden cross-partition broker transactions.
rationale: A hidden broker transaction hides its partial failures; an explicit saga leaves every step and every compensation in the log where a replay can see it.

sources.section: §7.1 Wire, ordering and delivery semantics — Atomicity ('Cross-partition business transactions are represented as sagas/commands, not hidden broker transactions')

verification.check: Inspection of the fabric API finds no multi-partition transaction primitive, and each cross-partition flow in the platform has a documented saga with a replay test of its compensation path.

notes: Split from the §7.1 Atomicity bullet.

title: Credit/window flow control paces every session
statement: The fabric must use credit/window flow control on every session, so a sender transmits only within credit its receiver has granted.
rationale: Without receiver-granted credit, the only backpressure is a full buffer somewhere, and the buffer that fills is usually the broker's.

sources.section: §7.1 Wire, ordering and delivery semantics — Backpressure ('credit/window flow control')

verification.check: Stop a consumer from granting credit and assert the broker sends nothing beyond the outstanding window; likewise a producer beyond its window is paused rather than buffered without bound.

notes: Split from §7.1's backpressure bullet (quotas are FABRIC-049, bounded queues FABRIC-063, priority FABRIC-051).

title: P0 control payloads are signed and verified before they are acted on
statement: Every P0 Critical Control payload must be signed by its authorised producer, and every consumer must verify the signature against the expected signer before acting on it, refusing an unsigned or badly signed record.
rationale: ACLs stop an unauthorised writer at the broker; a signature lets the cell itself prove who issued a risk envelope, including after a broker or mirror has handled it.

sources.section: §7.2 Fabric topic classes — P0 Critical Control row ('signed payload')

verification.check: Deliver a validly signed, an unsigned and a wrongly signed risk envelope to a paper Reflex cell and assert only the first is applied and the other two are refused and journaled.

notes: Split from the §7.2 P0 row. ADR 0043: asymmetric signing is one of the three gaps no in-tree code may close, so until a record admits a signing primitive this is scored blocked; an HMAC-keyed assertion (in-tree HMAC is authorised by ADR 0002) authenticates a shared-key producer but is not a signature a consumer can verify without holding the signing key. Package artifacts are signed separately (FABRIC-053).

title: The ledger sink retries indefinitely and never drops a financial outcome
statement: The ledger sink consuming P1 Financial Outcomes must retry a failed commit indefinitely with backoff, never skipping or dropping the record, and must not advance its offset past a record until that record is committed; its retries and lag must be observable.
rationale: A ledger that skips an outcome it could not write is wrong forever and silently; retrying indefinitely is safe only because commits are idempotent (FABRIC-044) and P1 retention outlasts an outage (FABRIC-046).

sources.section: §7.2 Fabric topic classes — P1 Financial Outcomes row ('ledger sink retries indefinitely')

verification.check: Deny writes to the ledger store for a sustained interval and assert the sink's committed offset does not advance, no P1 record is skipped, the retry and lag metrics move, and on restore every outcome commits once in effect (v2.1 §25 ledger-outage game day).

notes: Split from the §7.2 P1 row. 'Retries and lag must be observable' is the house observability rule: an indefinite retry nobody can see is an outage nobody knows about.

title: Market-journal mirroring is throttled before local ingest
statement: Under pressure, mirroring of P2 Market Journal topics must be throttled before local P2 ingest is slowed.
rationale: Local ingest is what the region's own replay and cells depend on; a remote copy of the market journal is worth less than the local original.

sources.section: §7.2 Fabric topic classes — P2 Market Journal row ('throttles mirror before local ingest')

verification.check: Saturate a broker with P2 ingest while mirroring and assert mirror throughput drops first and local append latency stays within budget.

notes: Split from the §7.2 P2 row. Only P2 is stated; P0 and P1 mirrors are critical and are not named as throttled first. MANAGED_SERVICE (the row's GCS archive) is removed as inapplicable. P1 with multi-region mirroring.

title: Production regions start with five broker VMs across three zones
statement: Each production region must initially run five C4D/C4-class broker VMs spread across three zones; three is the minimum, and five provides maintenance headroom and reduces correlated quorum pressure.
rationale: v2.1's stated reason: with three brokers, one in maintenance and one failed leaves no quorum; five keeps a quorum through both.

sources.section: §7.3 Fabric placement on GCP — Brokers ('five C4D/C4 VM instances per production region initially')

verification.check: terraform plan for a production region declares five C4D/C4-family broker instances across three zones, and a plan with fewer than three is refused by variable validation (the gate proven to refuse a bad value and admit a good one).

notes: Split from §7.3 Brokers, whose three-zone clause is FABRIC-008. ADR 0099 C8 records five brokers per region as blocked on an owner cost ceiling and a deployment record. The MVP's single-region three-broker topology is FABRIC-008.

title: Broker journals live on persistent Hyperdisk, with local SSD only as cache
statement: Broker journal disks must be persistent Hyperdisk sized for sustained append and read throughput; local SSD and page cache may be used only for transient acceleration.
rationale: A journal on local SSD disappears with its VM; persistent disk lets a replaced broker keep its log and shortens re-replication.

sources.section: §7.3 Fabric placement on GCP — Journal disks

verification.check: terraform plan attaches Hyperdisk journal volumes whose provisioned throughput meets the P2 class's sustained rate to every broker, and mounts any local SSD only as cache.

notes: Split from §7.3 Journal disks, whose durability clause is FABRIC-086. The diagram labels the segment store 'local PD / Local SSD cache' (H L206); v2.1's Hyperdisk is the more specific and is kept.

title: Journal durability derives from replication, never from one device
statement: No durability guarantee may depend on a single local device: a record counts as durable only when replicated as its class requires (FABRIC-077), and the loss of any one broker's disk must lose no acknowledged record.
rationale: Every disk fails eventually; a guarantee resting on one disk is a guarantee with a known expiry date nobody wrote down.

sources.section: §7.3 Fabric placement on GCP — Journal disks ('Durability derives from replicated journal, not one local device')

verification.check: Destroy one broker's journal disk and its local cache under load and assert every acknowledged record remains readable and the broker is rebuilt from replicas.

notes: Stated twice in the raw extraction. MANAGED_SERVICE and COST (the disk choice) stay with FABRIC-085.

title: Clients bootstrap from Cloud DNS SRV records
statement: Fabric clients must find bootstrap broker endpoints through Cloud DNS SRV records, optionally backed by Service Directory.
rationale: Hard-coded broker addresses break on the first broker replacement; SRV bootstrap lets the fleet change without redeploying clients.

sources.section: §7.3 Fabric placement on GCP — Discovery ('Cloud DNS SRV records and optionally Service Directory provide bootstrap endpoints')

verification.check: terraform plan declares a private Cloud DNS zone with SRV records for each region's fabric bootstrap endpoints, and a client configured only with the SRV name connects.

notes: Split from §7.3 Discovery, whose live-map half is FABRIC-088. v2.1's service catalogue Cloud DNS row ('Fabric bootstrap SRV', G p17) says the same.

title: Clients take the live broker and partition map from fabric metadata
statement: After bootstrap, clients must obtain the live broker/partition map from fabric metadata, not from DNS, and must send each partition's records to that partition's current leader, refreshing the map when leadership changes; a Reflex Node therefore holds a session to every broker that leads one of its partitions.
rationale: DNS is cached and slow to change; a client that routes by DNS after a failover writes to a follower or to nothing.

sources.section: §7.3 Fabric placement on GCP — Discovery ('clients obtain the live broker/partition map from Fabric metadata')
§02 Regional Cell — algorik-node → Broker A, B and C data edges

verification.check: Move a partition's leadership while a producer is active and assert the producer's next send goes to the new leader after a map refresh, with no DNS change, and that no record is sent to a follower.

notes: Merges the diagram's node-to-all-three-brokers edges, which the raw extraction read as the node writing every record to all three brokers 'not only to a single partition leader'. That reading would make the producer do replication, contradicting v2.1 §7.1 (G p8: leaders replicate to followers), which governs how the system runs; the edges are read here as the node holding a session to each broker because each leads some of its partitions. The conflict is recorded rather than resolved silently.

title: Brokers have stable internal addresses and no public endpoint
statement: Every broker must have a stable internal address and no public endpoint or external IP.
rationale: A public broker endpoint puts control topics one credential leak away from the internet.

sources.section: §7.3 Fabric placement on GCP — IP identity ('stable internal addresses, no public broker endpoints')

verification.check: terraform plan shows a static internal address on every broker and no external IP, public load balancer or firewall rule admitting 0.0.0.0/0 to any broker port.

notes: Split from §7.3 IP identity; MANAGED_SERVICE and MULTI_REGION move with its NCC half to FABRIC-052.

title: Archived segments are content-addressed in regional landing buckets
statement: Each closed segment must be written to its region's Cloud Storage landing bucket under a content address (its hash), so an archived object's name proves its content.
rationale: A content address makes re-archiving idempotent and tampering evident without a separate index of hashes.

sources.section: §7.3 Fabric placement on GCP — Archival ('closed segments are content-addressed and written to regional GCS landing buckets')

verification.check: Archive segments to a landing-bucket fake and assert every object name equals the hash of its bytes, re-archiving the same segment is a no-op, and a tampered object fails the name check.

notes: Split from §7.3 Archival (stated twice in the raw extraction), whose residency half is FABRIC-091.

title: Archived segments move to research/archive locations only as residency policy allows
statement: Segments must be lifecycled or copied from regional landing buckets to durable research/archive locations only as the applicable data-residency policy allows.
rationale: Market data and execution history can carry jurisdictional residency obligations; a lifecycle rule that copies across a boundary is a compliance breach done by automation.

sources.section: §7.3 Fabric placement on GCP — Archival ('lifecycle/copied to durable research/archive locations according to residency policy')

verification.check: terraform plan shows lifecycle and copy rules from each landing bucket only to locations the residency policy permits for that region, and a fixture policy forbidding a destination removes that rule.

notes: Split from §7.3 Archival. P1 with the data plane (GCP Phase 5).

title: Brokers are scaled deliberately, partitions ahead of peak — never by reactive autoscaling
statement: Fabric capacity must be scaled by adding brokers and rebalancing leaders and followers, and by increasing partitions per domain ahead of expected peaks; brokers must not be autoscaled reactively like stateless pods.
rationale: Adding a broker moves partitions, which costs replication bandwidth at the moment load is highest; reactive scaling does that work exactly when it hurts most.

sources.section: §7.3 Fabric placement on GCP — Scaling
§18 Scaling and Performance Model — Fabric row ('Add brokers, move leaders/followers, increase partitions by domain')

verification.check: terraform plan attaches no autoscaler to the broker instance group, and a rebalance drill adding one broker moves leaderships with no loss of acknowledged records.

notes: Merges §7.3 Scaling with the §18 Fabric row's scale unit. The row's headroom clause is FABRIC-101.

title: Brokers are upgraded one at a time: drain, verify, replace, rejoin, advance
statement: Broker upgrades must proceed one broker at a time: drain its leadership, verify replica health, replace its immutable image or binary, let it rejoin, and only then advance to the next.
rationale: An upgrade is a planned failure; doing it one broker at a time, with health verified in between, keeps it from becoming an unplanned one.

sources.section: §7.3 Fabric placement on GCP — Upgrade

verification.check: Rolling-upgrade a three-zone test cluster under live traffic and assert no two brokers are ever out of service together, replica health is verified before each advance, and no acknowledged record is lost.

notes: Split from §7.3 Upgrade, whose quorum prohibition is FABRIC-094. v2.1 §14.2 step 9 (G p13, 'Reflex/Fabric use component-specific drain/stage/epoch') says the same and is left to CI/CD.

title: An upgrade never takes enough replicas down to lose quorum
statement: No upgrade or maintenance action may take down, at the same time, enough replicas of any partition or of the metadata quorum to lose quorum, and a rollout must refuse to advance while any partition is under-replicated.
rationale: A rollout that advances on schedule rather than on health will eventually take the last in-sync replica with it.

sources.section: §7.3 Fabric placement on GCP — Upgrade ('Never upgrade enough replicas simultaneously to lose quorum')

verification.check: With one partition under-replicated, attempt to advance the rollout and assert it refuses; a property test over rollout schedules asserts no schedule the controller accepts ever leaves a partition or the metadata quorum below quorum.

notes: Split from §7.3 Upgrade. The refusal while under-replicated is the house fail-closed reading. P0 as a safety invariant.

title: Fabric consumers and sinks run on dedicated node pools
statement: Fabric consumers and sink workers must run on dedicated GKE node pools that no other warm service shares.
rationale: A sink catching up after an outage is a CPU and network burst; on a shared pool it starves the warm services that compute risk envelopes.

sources.section: §8 Regional GKE Service Plane — Fabric consumers/sinks row ('Dedicated node pools')

verification.check: terraform plan and the workload manifests place every sink and consumer on a dedicated, tainted node pool that no other workload tolerates.

notes: Split from the §8 row, whose lag-scaling and isolation clauses are FABRIC-096 and FABRIC-097. ADR 0099 C3: GKE was retired for Cloud Run (ADR 0024), and until a runtime record decides this is scored against the Cloud Run shape, where the equivalent is a dedicated service per sink.

title: Sink and consumer capacity scales on consumer lag
statement: Fabric consumer and sink capacity must scale on consumer lag, up to the partition count, rather than on CPU alone.
rationale: A sink waiting on a slow destination uses little CPU while falling hours behind; lag is the signal that measures the thing that matters.

sources.section: §8 Regional GKE Service Plane — Fabric consumers/sinks row ('Scale from consumer lag')

verification.check: Grow a sink's lag past its scaling threshold and assert the autoscaler adds consumers up to the partition count and removes them once lag drains.

notes: Split from the §8 row. Needs the lag metric emitted by FABRIC-072. P1 with GCP Phase 6 (Fabric consumer scaling).

title: Each sink's failure and backpressure are isolated from the others
statement: Each sink (Spanner, Bigtable, BigQuery, GCS) must have its own consumer, backpressure and failure isolation, so one slow or failing destination cannot stall any other sink.
rationale: A BigQuery quota error must not delay the ledger sink; a single shared throttle would make the slowest destination everyone's pace.

sources.section: §8 Regional GKE Service Plane — Fabric consumers/sinks row ('destination-specific failure isolation')
VIEWS.regional — 02 · Regional Cell, node 'sink' ('Spanner/Bigtable/BQ/GCS sinks with independent backpressure')

verification.check: Freeze the BigQuery destination fake and assert the Spanner, Bigtable and GCS sinks keep their throughput and lag unchanged.

notes: Merges the §8 row's isolation clause with the diagram's per-sink backpressure. Distinct from FABRIC-069 (sink versus broker). KUBERNETES (the §8 placement) is removed as inapplicable to the isolation property.

title: A lost broker is replaced and partitions rebalanced back to full replication
statement: After a broker failure, the broker must be replaced from its immutable image and partitions rebalanced so that every durable partition returns to RF3 across three zones without data loss.
rationale: After a failover the cluster runs one failure from losing quorum; restoration is what returns it to the state its guarantees assume.

sources.section: §17 Availability, Resilience and Disaster Recovery — Fabric broker row (recovery: 'replace broker and rebalance')

verification.check: Kill a broker permanently, run the replacement procedure, and assert every durable partition returns to three in-sync replicas across three zones with no loss of acknowledged records.

notes: Split from the §17 broker row; the failover half is FABRIC-055 and the preserved-records half FABRIC-077.

title: Critical mirrored topics stay readable elsewhere when a region's fabric is lost
statement: When an entire regional fabric is lost, its critical mirrored topics (control and outcomes) must remain readable in other regions, up to the mirror lag at the moment of loss.
rationale: Mirroring exists for this case: without it, the loss of one region's fabric would erase what the rest of the platform knew about that region's outcomes.

sources.section: §17 Availability, Resilience and Disaster Recovery — Entire Fabric region row ('critical mirrored topics available elsewhere')

verification.check: Remove one region's fabric in a multi-region staging game day and assert its mirrored P0 and P1 topics are readable in each surviving region up to the recorded mirror lag.

notes: Split from the region-loss row. Its 'GKE async workflows lose local bus' is a consequence rather than a requirement and is dropped as narrative. Reflex continuing under cached policy is FABRIC-054 and healthy regions continuing FABRIC-021. NEW_DEPENDENCY is removed as inapplicable.

title: A lost regional fabric is rebuilt from surviving replicas and GCS archives
statement: A lost regional fabric must be rebuildable from surviving replicas and its Cloud Storage segment archive while healthy regions continue.
rationale: A region that cannot be rebuilt from what survived is a region whose history was lost with it.

sources.section: §17 Availability, Resilience and Disaster Recovery — Entire Fabric region row (recovery: 'Bring region back from surviving replicas/GCS archives')

verification.check: Rebuild a nonprod regional fabric from zero using only Terraform, surviving replicas and its archive (v2.1 §25's rebuild-from-zero drill, G p22) and assert every archived offset range is present and consumers resume.

notes: Split from the region-loss row.

title: Fabric keeps capacity headroom for a zone loss and for maintenance
statement: Fabric capacity must keep enough headroom to absorb the loss of one zone and a broker under maintenance at peak load.
rationale: Headroom sized for normal operation fails on the day a zone goes during a maintenance window, which is the day it was bought for.

sources.section: §18 Scaling and Performance Model — Fabric row ('keep headroom for zone loss and maintenance')

verification.check: With one zone's brokers removed and one further broker drained, fabric-bench at the recorded peak rate keeps every class within its latency budget.

notes: Split from the §18 Fabric row, whose scale-unit clause is FABRIC-092.

title: Eventarc is not part of core internal eventing
statement: Eventarc must not be used for core internal eventing; it may be used only for peripheral Google-service automation that does not become an application dependency.
rationale: An Eventarc trigger is a second event path with its own delivery semantics; once an application depends on it, the fabric no longer defines internal eventing.

sources.section: §19.1 Deliberately not used as core internal messaging — Eventarc row

verification.check: An architecture test fails if any workspace service is the target of an Eventarc trigger, and inspection of Terraform finds Eventarc triggers only on peripheral automation targets.

notes: P1: a GCP-plane exclusion that matters once warm services exist.

title: Cloud Tasks is not an internal general queue
statement: Cloud Tasks must not be used as an internal general-purpose queue; it may be used only by isolated customer-facing workflows whose task semantics specifically fit.
rationale: A general queue beside the fabric splits internal work across two delivery models, and the one without replay becomes where things are lost.

sources.section: §19.1 Deliberately not used as core internal messaging — Cloud Tasks row

verification.check: An architecture test fails if any internal service enqueues to, or is invoked by, Cloud Tasks outside an allow-list of isolated customer-facing workflows.

notes: P1: a GCP-plane exclusion.

title: Regional warm services publish policy, envelopes, grants and research events to the fabric
statement: Regional warm (GKE) services must publish policy, risk-envelope and capital-grant events as P0 control, the financial outcome events they originate (such as settlement events) as P1, and research, world and knowledge events as P3, to their regional fabric asynchronously.
rationale: Control that reaches cells by any path other than the fabric has no offset, no replay and no record of issue; research events published the same way become replayable inputs to learning.

title: Regional warm services consume ordered partitions from the fabric in consumer groups
statement: Regional warm services — Risk Brain, Capital/Treasury, Asset/Strategy, Evidence/World Model, Ambient/Causal agents and the sink workers — must consume the fabric's ordered partitions by asynchronous pull/stream in consumer groups, with replay.
rationale: Consuming from the fabric, rather than from each other, is what lets warm services scale, restart and be replayed independently of the cells that produced their inputs.

title: The archiver reaches Cloud Storage over private Google API access
statement: fabric-archive must write to Cloud Storage only through private Google API access, with no public-internet path.
rationale: Archived segments carry financial outcomes and licensed market data; a public path exposes them in transit and needs egress the fabric network should not have.

sources.section: §20 Critical Service-to-Service Connection Matrix — Fabric Archive → Cloud Storage row ('Google API private access')

verification.check: terraform plan enables Private Google Access (or a PSC endpoint) on the fabric subnet with no NAT or external route the archiver could use, and an archiver run with only the private path succeeds.

title: The Bigtable sink maintains recent features, time series and replay indexes
statement: A Bigtable sink must consume fabric partitions asynchronously and maintain recent features, time series and replay indexes in Bigtable over gRPC.
rationale: Warm services and replay need recent features at a rate a log scan cannot serve; a sink keeps that derived state current from the log it is derived from.

sources.section: §20 Critical Service-to-Service Connection Matrix — Fabric Bigtable Sink row
§21.1 Tick to order and learning — step 4 ('update recent features in Bigtable')

title: The BigQuery sink streams research and analytics data and may lag
statement: A BigQuery sink must stream research and analytics records to BigQuery through the Storage Write API asynchronously, and its lag must have no trading impact.
rationale: Analytics is the most delay-tolerant consumer; the requirement that it may lag is what lets it never be allowed to slow anything that trades.

notes: ADR 0099 C4 and C2 govern, as for FABRIC-107. P1 with the data plane (GCP Phase 5).

title: Warm services receive Reflex outputs only through the fabric
statement: Regional warm services must receive Reflex Cell outcomes, journals and decision traces only through the fabric, never by a direct connection to a Reflex Cell.
rationale: A direct service-to-cell connection is a dependency the cell has to serve, which puts warm-service load on the hot host and bypasses the log.

verification.check: An architecture test asserts no warm-service crate opens a connection to a Reflex or edge-node endpoint, and inspection of firewall rules finds no service-to-Reflex ingress.

title: Ambient and development agents publish only at P3/P4
statement: Ambient and development agents must publish their research, operations and engineering events into the fabric at the P3 Intelligence/Research and P4 Telemetry classes only, and ACLs must refuse them P0 control and P1 outcome topics.
rationale: An agent that can write a control topic can escalate its own authority; confining agents to P3/P4 keeps their output as evidence for decisions rather than decisions.

title: The release/package controller announces activations as P0 control through Fabric Meta
statement: Model, policy and package activation announcements must be published by the Release/Package Controller, and by no other producer, as P0 critical-control records admitted through Fabric Meta's schema, ACL and producer-fencing authority.
rationale: Package activation changes what every cell runs. One accountable publisher, fenced and schema-checked, is what makes an activation attributable to an approved release.
